author: ohtadmin
title: POW/MIAs to be honored Sept. 19
text:
In 1998, Congress declared the third Friday in September to be National POW/MIA Recognition Day, which honors Americans who were prisoners of war or still missing in action.
More than 81,000 Americans have fallen into those categories since the start of World War II, with half being sailors and airmen whose ships and planes went down in the Pacific Ocean.
The Arnold-Zweir Post of the American Legion and the VFW Post 9447 will fly a POW/MIA flag Friday, Sept. 19, in Veterans Memorial Square at East Ferry in memory of Weeden, Closson, Sweet and Grevette.
The flag also will honor the tens of thousands of other Americans who have been captured by enemy forces or gone missing during combat.
Two men from Jamestown became prisoners of war. According to the Beavertail Lighthouse Museum Association, Welcome Weeden, whose ancestors had been in Jamestown for seven generations, was appointed keeper of the Beavertail Lighthouse in January 1862 by Abraham Lincoln. He had the post for nine months then moved to Fall River, Mass., with his wife and two children.
On Feb. 16, 1864, Weeden joined the 58th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment. He mustered as a private with Company G when he was 28 and departed Massachusetts for Virginia with his regiment in April 1864.
On May 6, the 58th regiment went into action in the Battle of the Wilderness followed by the Battle of Spotsylvania Courthouse, where Weeden was captured May 19, 1864, which was the final day of that 13-day battle.
Weeden was sent as a prisoner to the overcrowded, unsanitary Andersonville Prison in Georgia, where he died of disease July 13, 1864. He is buried in the Andersonville National Cemetery with the 13,000 fellow Union prisoners who also died at the prison. That is more than one-quarter of the 45,000 prisoners sent to Andersonville during the Civil War.
Archie Closson, born in 1928, came to Jamestown with his family in 1937 when he was in elementary school. They lived on Maple Avenue and his father worked at the torpedo factory on Goat Island. Closson was friends with Donald Richardson, who still lives in Jamestown.
Pvt. Closson was stationed in Japan with the Army’s 21st Infantry Regiment in June 1950 when the North Korean People’s Army invaded South Korea. Closson’s regiment, understrength and short of equipment, were the first American troops sent to Korea. They were badly outnumbered as units were pushed back and surrounded.
On July 12, a week after his arrival, Closson was among the soldiers in the 21st Regiment to be captured by the North Koreans. A group of 850 American prisoners of war were marched north, and as the weather got colder, they still were wearing their ragged summer uniforms.
By the end of October, 92 of the 850 had died. Although some were executed, most died from malnutrition, disease and the cold.
Forces with the United Nations, which had begun attacking the North Koreans, pushed them northward. The enemy took their prisoners with them, including Closson, and the Americans endured the 120-mile “Tiger Death March” through the snow.
The dwindling group spent most of the winter at the Hanjang-ni POW camp near the Chinese border, which is where Closson died March 21, 1951, eight months and nine days after he was captured. He was 22 years old.
When the armistice was signed, and the POWs were released in August 1953, only 262 soldiers from Closson’s original group of 850, 31 percent, remained alive.
Closson’s parents are buried in Middletown. His remains have not yet been recovered. While the U.S. Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency continues to search for his body, cooperation from North Korea is sporadic.
Two other Jamestown men are missing in action from World War II.
William Sweet, who was born in Jamestown in 1924, moved to Newport with his family when he was in elementary school. He enlisted in the Army Air Force, four months after graduating from Rogers High School in 1942, and began training to serve on C-47 transport planes. Sweet, however, successfully asked to be reassigned to bombers.
After training as a flight engineer, Sweet was sent by way of North Africa to Italy in July 1944, where his crew joined the 513th Squadron of the 376th Bombardment Group (Heavy), flying four-engine long-range B-24 Liberator bombers.
The crew already had flown 17 missions when, on Sept. 10, 1944, they took off to bomb an ordnance plant in Vienna, Austria. According to the bombardier on the mission, “the Vienna .ak was heavy, intense, and accurate.” It ripped holes in both wings. Flying back to Italy with gasoline leaking from the wings and a damaged fuel distribution system, the plane ran out of fuel halfway across the Adriatic Sea.
All 10 crew members parachuted into the sea. Sweet, who was responsible for the proper operation of the engines, was the second to last to leave the plane. He was one of the farthest down the 10-mile path that the plane traveled during the evacuation.
Most of the crew were found by an Italian fishing boat. Only Sweet and the turret gunner went missing in the rough sea.
Delbert Grevette, born in Jamestown, joined the U.S. Navy as a first-class ship’s cook aboard the USS Buck in the Mediterranean Sea. Just after midnight Oct. 9, 1943, while patrolling off the west coast of Italy near Salerno, the American destroyer was torpedoed by the German submarine U-616 and sank in four minutes. Ninety-seven survivors were rescued the next morning, but Grevette was not among them. He was lost when the ship went down. Grevette is still considered missing in action.
